result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.resistance_distance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Calculate the resistance distance between two nodes. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.resistance_distance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Calculate the resistance distance between two nodes. title: >- [Graph.resistance_distance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Calculate the resistance distance between two nodes. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate the resistance distance between two nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L73332-L73463){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.resistance_distance( source, target, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Resistance distance](/assets/graphs/resistance-distance.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Nodes A and B are outlined in the accent color and joined by two routes drawn in accent, A–C–B and A–D–E–B, with each edge a 1 ohm resistor. The card combines the 2 and 3 ohm routes in parallel, 2·3 / (2+3), for a resistance of 1.2." width="100%"} The resistance distance (also called effective resistance) is the electrical resistance between two nodes if each edge is replaced by a 1-ohm resistor. It is a metric on graphs that satisfies the triangle inequality and provides insight into network connectivity and robustness. Unlike shortest-path distance, which only looks at the single best route, resistance distance accounts for *all* routes between two nodes. Edges along one path add up like resistors in series, and alternative paths lower the resistance like resistors in parallel. Two nodes joined by many independent routes are "closer" than two nodes joined by one route of the same length. This makes it useful for: - measuring how robustly two nodes are connected (low resistance means many redundant routes) - estimating random-walk quantities, since the commute time between two nodes is proportional to their resistance distance - link prediction and node similarity, where well-connected pairs are more likely to be related Edge weights are ignored (every edge is a 1-ohm resistor). Parallel edges act as resistors in parallel, so two edges between the same nodes give a resistance of `0.5`. Self-loops are ignored. If the two nodes are in different connected components, no current can flow between them and the result is `float("inf")`. Each call does an `O(m^3)` matrix computation on the component containing the two nodes (`m` nodes); when you need many pairs, `resistance_distance_matrix()` computes them all at once for the cost of a single call. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The first node, given as an integer node ID or a string label. The node must exist in the graph. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The second node, given as an integer node ID or a string label. The node must exist in the graph. Because resistance distance is symmetric, swapping `source=` and `target=` gives the same result. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The resistance distance between the two nodes (non-negative, at most the shortest-path hop distance). Returns `0.0` if source equals target, and `float("inf")` if they are in different connected components. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed (resistance distance is only defined for undirected graphs). [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If either source or target node doesn't exist in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Effective resistance treats the graph as an electrical network where every edge is a 1-ohm resistor and reports the voltage that would develop between $u$ and $v$ when one unit of current is injected at $u$ and extracted at $v$. This yields a proper metric $\Omega$ satisfying the triangle inequality, and it exposes global connectivity: $\Omega(u, v) \le 1$ for any pair joined by an edge, with equality holding *only* when that edge is a bridge (its removal disconnects the graph). The metric has a random-walk interpretation via the Chandra-Raghavan-Ruzzo-Smolensky commute-time formula $C(u, v) = 2m \cdot \Omega(u, v)$, where $m = |E|$; that identity makes $\Omega$ a natural fit for algorithms that reason about mixing times. It is computed as $\Omega(u, v) = L^+_{uu} + L^+_{vv} - 2 L^+_{uv}$ from the Laplacian pseudoinverse $L^+$, at a cost of $O(n^3)$ per call. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Between two directly connected nodes in a simple graph, the resistance distance is exactly 1.0, matching a single 1-ohm resistor: ::: {#55f17b8c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph() g.add_full_graph(2) # Returns 1.0 g.resistance_distance(1, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1.0000000000000002 ``` ::: ::: On a path, resistors are effectively in series, so resistance distance grows linearly with the number of edges between two nodes (tiny floating-point differences are expected): ::: {#65f85d9c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = ec.Graph() path.add_path_graph(4) # 1-2-3-4 # Returns about (1.0, 2.0, 3.0): resistance grows with the number of edges between nodes ( path.resistance_distance(1, 2), path.resistance_distance(1, 3), path.resistance_distance(1, 4), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1.0, 1.9999999999999996, 2.9999999999999987) ``` ::: ::: A cycle offers two parallel paths between any pair of nodes, which lowers the effective resistance compared to a single path of the same length: ::: {#39ba8b8f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} cycle = ec.Graph() cycle.add_cycle_graph(4) # 1-2-3-4-1 # Returns about 0.75: parallel paths of length 1 and 3 give 1 * 3 / (1 + 3) cycle.resistance_distance(1, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0.7500000000000001 ``` ::: ::: Nodes can also be given by label. Both `A`-`B` and `C1`-`D` are two hops apart, but `A` and `B` are joined by two independent routes, while every route from `C1` to `D` has to cross the single edge `B-D`. Shortest-path distance can't tell the pairs apart; resistance distance gives `1.0` versus `1.75`: ::: {#963b2987 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C1", "C2", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "C1"), ("C1", "B"), ("A", "C2"), ("C2", "B"), ("B", "D")]) ) (g.resistance_distance("A", "B"), g.resistance_distance("C1", "D")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (1.0, 1.7499999999999998) ``` ::: :::
